The general form of the problem is the one §8.5 spent three editions getting wrong: these machines agree about how long a second lasts and they do not agree about what time it is.

So the wire carries an age. A node says “I saw this 47 seconds ago”, which is a duration, and the asking node stamps it against its own clock on arrival:

;;; answer: 'o <id>|<label>|<conf>|<age> ...'
sane_age((now - subscrv(4, r)) / 1000000.0) -> age;
nextif(age > max_age);

This needs no NTP, no offset estimation and no shared epoch. It is the same correction swarm.p needed, one layer up.

Fixing the clock is not a reason to undo this

The Pi’s NTP was later repaired — it now measures +0.16+0.16 s against this machine, inside the ssh round trip. That is not an argument for putting timestamps back on the wire. A disciplined clock still steps, forwards and back, and a design should not depend on a daemon being healthy on every node.

The repair in fact introduced a failure mode the Pi did not have while it was merely wrong: a backward step makes an age negative, which sails straight through an “older than the window?” test and reports a sighting from the future, while a forward step expires the whole store at once. swarm.p already guarded its dt against exactly this; sightnet.p did not, until fixing the clock made it reachable. sane_age/1 now clamps both ends.

8.7.2 Expiry is the owner’s job

A node prunes its own store and nobody prunes anyone else’s. A sighting that nobody ever asks for still expires. SIGHT_TTL defaults to a day and is overridable, because a 24-hour boundary that cannot be demonstrated without waiting 24 hours is a boundary nobody checks:

SIGHT_TTL=86400 -> seeded 7 sightings, 6 survive   (one was 25h old)
SIGHT_TTL=600   -> seeded 7 sightings, 3 survive

8.7.3 Dedup by sequence, not by content

Each robot numbers its own sightings. A requestor remembers the highest sequence it has seen from each robot and sends those marks with the query, so the reply carries only what is new — which also keeps it inside one datagram. Hashing the content instead would collide the moment two frames of the same quiet corridor looked alike, and a fleet would go blind exactly where nothing was happening.

The watcher shows it: the first poll returns the backlog, and every poll after returns precisely one new row per node per reel tick, never a repeat.

** ALERT cat (0.91 confidence) seen 22.0 s ago -- r2-1
8 new rows, 2 alerts
2 new rows, 0 alerts
2 new rows, 0 alerts
** ALERT cat (0.86 confidence) seen 0.5 s ago -- r2-14
2 new rows, 2 alerts

8.7.4 Prolog asks, Pop-11 holds

The store is mutable and expiring, which is exactly why Pop-11 owns it and Prolog reads it through a define :prolog predicate — one heap, no marshalling, no serialisation boundary. Local store and remote fleet are reached the same way, so the rules cannot tell them apart:

sighting(Id,R,L,C,A) :- local_sighting(Id,R,L,C,A).
sighting(Id,R,L,C,A) :- remote_sighting(Id,R,L,C,A).

recently(Id,R,L,C,A) :- sighting(Id,R,L,C,A), A =< 300.
today(Id,R,L,C,A)    :- sighting(Id,R,L,C,A), A =< 86400.

Verified across three machines and three architectures, with macOS arm64 asking and a Linux box and a Pi serving. A frame behind a sighting can be fetched too, in as many signed chunks as it takes — the same mechanism examples/robotarmy/deploy.p uses for source, and byte-identical on arrival.

8.8 A classifier small enough to be honest

The labels above were canned. examples/robotarmy/vision.p makes them real, with a network trained in Pop-11 rather than imported from somewhere else — and the interesting decision is how small it is.

A 256→16→4256 \rightarrow 16 \rightarrow 4 network cannot tell a cat from a dog in a photograph. Nothing that size can, and a transformer over image patches would be slower and no better. What it can do is recognise a small fixed vocabulary of markers under controlled conditions, which is what a fleet watching for painted signs actually needs. So the classes are shapes, and what a shape means is left to Prolog, where it is data:

means(circle, cat).      means(triangle, hazard).
alarming(cat).           alarming(hazard).

suspicious(Id,R,M,A) :- recently(Id,R,Shape,C,A), C >= 0.8,
                        means(Shape,M), alarming(M).

A live fleet can be taught a new sign, or a new alarm, with examples/robotarmy/deploy.p and no restart. The accuracy below is real but easy by construction — four well-separated shapes, jittered in position and size, with light sensor noise. Saying so is part of reporting it.

8.8.1 Train through the graph, infer without it

Two measurements decided the shape of this. Training runs through the scalar autograd of examples/robotarmy/examples/microgpt/microgpt.p — a Pop-11 port of Karpathy’s micrograd — at 275 samples/second: fine for 240 samples, hopeless for anything real, so we train once, twelve epochs in ten seconds.

Inference does not need the graph at all. A Value carries its children and their local derivatives so that v_backward can walk them; none of that is wanted to answer “what is this?”. Dropping it for plain floats measured a 30×\times speedup, with another 23% from fast_subscrv, which skips the bounds check:

classifications/sec
macOS arm64 9121
Linux x86-64 7717
Pi aarch64 3417

All three report 100% held-out accuracy and identical confidences to six decimal places. Same weights, same answers, three architectures — which is the assurance that matters after a chapter’s worth of arithmetic bugs.

Weights are data, not code

The first version of the exporter wrote weights as Pop-11 source, making the compiler build a 4096-element literal to get 4096 numbers into a vector. That is the wrong mechanism on its own terms — and on the Pi it also turned out to be a way to crash the engine with SIGILL, reproducibly, on files that macOS arm64 and Linux x86-64 compile without complaint.

The failing set is non-monotonic: 500 floats pass, 550 through 2500 fail, 3000 and above pass again. It moves when popdprecision changes. The same file crashes one program and not another. That looks more like heap-layout-dependent corruption than a code-generator threshold, but it is not diagnosed, and examples/robotarmy/docs/bugs/aarch64-large-literal-sigill.md says so rather than guessing in the reader’s direction.

Weights are now written as plain numbers and read back with line_repeater and strnumber. That works everywhere, loads faster, and is what should have been done first.

8.8.2 What the fleet sees

With weights present, sightnet.p’s reel stops inventing labels: it renders a frame, classifies it, and records the network’s answer. A fetch returns the frame that was actually classified, so a requestor can pull the evidence rather than take the label on trust.

[reel] r1 saw circle (drawn circle, 0.99 confidence), 1 held
r1-5 / cat / 3.7          <- saw/4: shape resolved to meaning
r1-3 / hazard / 11.8

Which is the whole arrangement in three lines: a network says what shape it saw, Prolog says what that shape means, and the fleet decides whether to care — each in the language that suits it, all in one process.

8.9 What this is really showing

Strip the theme away and the chapter makes one claim: the unit of deployment can be smaller than a program. A word, a procedure, a handful of VM instructions — signed, sent, compiled on arrival, live in a process that never stopped. The fleet is not running software that was installed; it is running software that arrived.

That is only practical because compiling is cheap enough to do casually (§1.2), because the compiler is a procedure in the running system rather than a separate program (§2.2), and because the VM’s back-ends make the same abstract code native on every port (Chapter 6). Take any one of those away and you are back to shipping containers.

9 Where to go next

9.1 The documentation you already have

The in-tree corpus is over 900 files and it is the primary source for everything in this book. From any prompt:

: help matches          ;;; practical, task-shaped
: ref  vmcode           ;;; the exhaustive reference -- and the VM spec
: teach json            ;;; tutorials, including how lib json was built

The same material is published at https://iotone.github.io/poplog/, regenerated on every push by a Pop-11 program; llms.txt there is for AI assistants. The handful of entries worth reading early: help external and ref external (Chapter 7), ref vmcode and ref subsystem (Chapter 6), ref regexp, help json, help crypto, and teach swank.

9.2 Four decades of teaching material

Poplog was the vehicle for a great deal of university AI teaching, and most of it survives. The tree does not vendor any of it; one script fetches it from public archives and wires it into help/teach inside the system:

tools/fetch-learning.sh list        # what's available
tools/fetch-learning.sh --all       # about 30 MB into learn/
hidden-gems Small idiomatic demos of what makes Pop-11 distinctive: the open stack, updaters, dynamic lists, coroutines, dlocal, the GC, extensible syntax.
bhamteach The Birmingham introductory-AI course — pattern-matching chatbots, grammars and parsing, story generation, recursion exercises.
packages The classic package tree: SimAgent and Poprulebase, popvision, rclib, neural nets, Braitenberg vehicles.
paradigms A UMASS programming-language-paradigms course taught in Pop-11 (1997–2000).
primer The Pop-11 Primer — the standard text for experienced programmers.
examples Curated teaching examples: Othello, Life, robolang.

Upstream licences apply per pack; each records its origin in learn/pack/.source.

9.3 Reading the source

Poplog is written mostly in itself, which makes it unusually approachable.

  • pop/src/ — the core: vm_plant.p and vm_control.p are the VM builder from Chapter 6; syscomp/ holds one directory per CPU back-end.

  • pop/lib/lib/ — the library, and the best source of idiomatic Pop-11 at length. json.p, crypto.p, http_server.p, jsonrpc.p, swank.p and forth.p are all readable in an afternoon each.

  • pop/plog/, pop/lisp/, pop/pml/, pop/forth/ — the four front-ends, i.e. four worked answers to Chapter 6.

  • examples/ — runnable programs: the HTTP service, ELIZA, a Z-machine interpreter, graphics demos.

9.4 Benchmarks, ports, and the state of the project

BENCHMARKS.md carries the full cross-platform, cross-language matrix with its methodology; the numbers quoted in Chapter 1 are drawn from it. The PORTING-*.md files are the working notes from the AArch64, Apple Silicon and RISC-V ports — including the bugs, which is the part usually missing from porting documentation and the part most useful to the next porter. Windows is the one platform still marked TODO.

If you take one idea away

It is that a compiler cheap enough to call in a loop changes what a command post can be. Everything distinctive here — live redefinition, saved images, five languages in one heap, an editor that talks to a running process, an agent that keeps a session warm across tool calls and teaches it new orders mid-mission — falls out of fifteen microseconds per definition. The full Robot Army is at examples/robotarmy/; start with fleet.p and give it an order.

Appendix A — Cheat sheet

Syntax

;;; text comment to end of line
value -> x assignment; the arrow points at the destination
expr => print the result(s), prefixed **
expr ==> as => but prints structure in full
npr(x) print x and a newline
a sys_>< b concatenate anything into a string
a >< b concatenate two strings
’text’ string (mutable, counted, not NUL-terminated)
"word" word — an interned symbol
[a b c] list; contents are quoted
[^x ^(e) ^^xs] …with x, e evaluated and xs spliced
{1 2 3} vector
[% e %]  {% e %} list/vector of everything e leaves on the stack
p(% a %) closure: p partially applied to a

Blocks — every opener has a closer

define f(a, b); …enddefine; if …then …elseif …else …endif
define f(a) -> r; …enddefine; unless …then …endunless
procedure(a); …endprocedure for i from 1 to n do …endfor
define :class C; slot s = v; enddefine; for x in list do …endfor
define :method m(x:C); …enddefine; while c do …endwhile
section $-name => exports; …endsection; repeat …quitif(c); …endrepeat
exload tag [libs] …endexload; switchon e case < 0 then …endswitchon

Declarations

vars permanent (global) — required for matcher pattern variables. lvars lexical local — the default choice inside a procedure. constant, lconstant their immutable forms. dlocal x = v rebind for the dynamic extent of the call, restored on any exit.

Mishap decoder

DECLARING VARIABLE x (a warning) you used an undefined name — usually a typo or a missing define
NUMBER(S) NEEDED arithmetic on a non-number, often the value of that undefined name
STRING NEEDED a word "x" was passed where a string ’x’ was wanted — check the quotes
ILLEGAL DECLARATION OF WORD the name is already a protected system identifier; rename
MISPLACED EXPRESSION ITEM syntax: usually a missing keyword or a construct used with the wrong shape
EXECUTING NON-PROCEDURE calling something that is not a procedure — often an undefined name
CAN’T RESTORE - NOT SAME SYSTEM AND VERSION the .psv image predates the current basepop11; rebuild the images
sysEXECUTE: NOT AT EXECUTE LEVEL VM planting attempted at compile-time top level — wrap it in a procedure

Files, processes, tables

;;; read a file line by line
vars dev = sysopen('/path/file', 0, "line");
vars rep = line_repeater(dev, inits(4096));   ;;; buffer size = max line length
repeat
    rep() -> line;
    quitif(line == termin);
    if issubstring('ERROR', 1, line) then ... endif;
endrepeat;

sysobey('ls /tmp > /tmp/out');                          ;;; run a command
vars r = sys_obey_linerep('set +e; grep pat file');     ;;; ...and stream it

newproperty([], 50, false, true) -> tbl;   ;;; hash table, keys matched by ==
newmapping([],  50, false, true) -> m;     ;;; ...keys matched by =

line_repeater truncates lines longer than its buffer, so size inits(n) generously. sys_obey_linerep runs its command line under errexit: prefix set +e; whenever a failure is expected.

Regular expressions

The escape character is @; . * [ ] ^ $ are literal unless escaped; there is no alternation and no lookaround.

vars err, p;
regexp_compile('ERROR @[0-9@]@{1,@}') -> (err, p);   ;;; test err -- false = ok
p(1, 'ERROR 42 happened', false, false) -> (i, n);   ;;; -> 1  8
substring(i, n, 'ERROR 42 happened') =>              ;;; ** ERROR 42

Case-insensitive: regexp_compile(s, 1, false), or @i in the pattern. p is a compiled procedure — define it once, reuse it.

Datagrams

What Chapter 8 is built on. ‘i‘ is the internet domain and ‘D‘ a datagram socket; an address is a list, with * for INADDR_ANY.

uses unix_sockets;
vars sock = sys_socket(`i`, `D`, false);
[* 9951] -> sys_socket_name(sock);                 ;;; bind
sys_socket_send(sock, msg, length(msg), 0, ['127.0.0.1' 9952]);
vars buf = inits(2048);
sys_socket_recv(sock, buf, 2048, 0, true) -> (n, sender);
substring(1, n, buf) =>                            ;;; the payload

To poll, use sys_device_wait and not sys_input_waiting, which answers false forever on a datagram socket even with a datagram queued — a deaf poll that raises no error, because nothing arriving is also what a quiet network looks like (docs/bugs/sys-input-waiting-blind-on-sockets.md).

vars rd;
sys_device_wait([^sock], [], [], 0) -> (rd, , );    ;;; 0 = don't block
if rd /== [] then ... endif;

The Robot Army examples

All at examples/robotarmy/; each runs from the repository root.

File Ch. What it shows
fleet.p 3, 4 Robot class, word-keyed registry, muster() on the open stack, obey() on the matcher
telemetry.p, fleet.log 4 One-pass log triage: line_repeater, default-valued properties, @-regexps
c2.p 4 The command post: http_server + json over fleet.p
chain.pl 5 The chain of command in Prolog
patrol.fth 5 Robot control words in Forth, with an early leave
signed_orders.p 7 HMAC-signed orders through lib crypto
fleetnet.p 8 The UDP transport under everything networked: net_open/net_send/net_recv/net_poll, signed with HMAC-SHA256
orders.p 8 The fleet takes orders over the network — the same obey and registry, driven from another machine
fthwire.p 8 Forth over the wire: a robot is taught a word it has never seen, in one datagram, and runs it natively
deploy.p 8 Pop-11 source over the wire: signed, chunked, pop11_compiled into a running robot — including redefining a procedure already in use
plant.p 8 VM specs over the wire: sysPROCEDURE/sysPUSHQ/sysCALL, so one datagram becomes arm64 on one machine and x86-64 on another
swarm.p 8 Robots that fall into step: each broadcasts its phase and pulls towards the others, with no leader and no clock
chainnet.p 8 Backtracking across machines: the org chart split across nodes, put back together by Prolog’s own backtracking
sightnet.p 8 What the fleet has seen lately: sightings that expire, windowed and deduplicated, held by no one node
vision.p 8 A classifier small enough to be honest: trained in Pop-11 on real pixels, identical to six decimals on three architectures

./poplog basepop11 +target/psv/pml.psv Standard ML
tools/forth.sh Forth
